target_customer: Consumers with photos scattered across services who want one private library
problem: Photos live in many places (phone, Instagram, Flickr, Picasa, hard drives); Snapjoy imported them and organized them into albums by metadata.
business_model: Consumer subscription photo storage (pricing not found)

founders.name: Michael Dwan
founders.background_notes: YC bio: software designer and engineer in Colorado who builds developer tools.

founders.name: JP Ren
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page with no bio.

exit.reason: Dropbox stopped new signups after the deal; on 2013-06-22 Snapjoy told users it would shut down, with data export open until July 24, and gave no further reason.

competitors.name: Picasa Web Albums
competitors.what: Google photo organizing and hosting layer under Google+

technical_complexity.rationale: Importing from many photo sources, de-duplicating, and organizing by metadata at storage scale, plus an iOS app (TechCrunch 2012 covered a Timeline iOS viewer), was standard engineering with some hard parts.

defensibility.rationale: Users' stored libraries create some lock-in, but Flickr, Picasa and later Everpix and Dropbox offered close substitutes.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Dropbox acquired Snapjoy in December 2012 and shut it down in June 2013.

market_need_then: A 2011 Xconomy piece discussed what would come after Flickr and where photos would live in the cloud, which shows unmet demand for personal photo libraries.

branding.domain_note: Used snapjoy.com (exact .com); it now shows only the word Closed.

identity.voice_and_tone: Tagline described as a place to enjoy your photos (Built In Colorado)

brand_strength.rationale: Covered by TechCrunch and Engadget on acquisition and shutdown, but no source describes logo, community or brand-driven growth.

outcome_analysis: Snapjoy, a Boulder photo aggregation service from YC S11, was bought by Dropbox in December 2012, stopped taking new signups, and was shut down in June 2013 with a short notice to users. No company reason was given; TechCrunch speculated the deal was an acquihire or preparation for a Dropbox photo product, which is speculation, so no failure factor is asserted. Competition from Flickr, Picasa and well-funded photo startups was context.
notes: Funding rests on one database (CB Insights, $20K total, investors listed as Dropbox and Y Combinator with no round date or stage); Dropbox is likely listed as the acquirer, so only Y Combinator is recorded as investor. Acquisition price undisclosed. Status Inactive in the YC directory agrees with the shutdown after acquisition. Engadget acquisition article was seen in search results, not opened; the TechCrunch shutdown article was opened. Competitor sources are from a search snippet of an Xconomy article dated 2011-08-26.
